cim: Artificial Intelligence Streamlines Clinical Workflows and Patient Care for Family Physicians
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence Streamlines Clinical Workflows and Patient Care for Family Physicians
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming medicine and health care in unprecedented ways. As information systems increasingly integrate AI into daily workflows, clinicians are finding that its greatest value lies in restoring time for meaningful, empathetic patient engagement.

In a recent video interview, Michael Albert, MD, DABOM, Chief Medical Officer at Vineyard Health, highlighted how AI tools — ranging from plain-language summaries to custom electronic medical record (EMR)-integrated applications — can distill complex clinical data into digestible insights for patients while streamlining time-consuming administrative tasks.

I am Dr Michael Albert. I am an internist and diplomate of the American Board of Obesity Medicine (ABOM). I am the Chief Medical Officer at Vineyard Health, where I also handle business development and artificial intelligence (AI) utilization.

How can AI help bridge the gap between complex medical information and communicating with patients?

Michael Albert, MD, DABOM: One of the benefits of AI is that it helps to translate a lot of the data noise into digestible formats. One of the topics I discussed at the conference was how physicians can simplify information relevant to a patient’s history or medical case to match their reading and comprehension levels. Simple level-1 prompting can generate easy-to-read, plain-language summaries for patients. This is a basic yet highly useful way to leverage AI for patient communication.

What kinds of applications and trackers can AI help physicians create to assist in treating patients living with obesity?

Dr Albert: In our clinic, we are creating bespoke applications and plug-ins that integrate directly with our electronic medical record (EMR) system. These tools help patients better understand their biometric data, comprehend their health plans, and track their longitudinal progress. This is possible because modern coding agents and software architectures are simple to use. Nontechnical individuals can leverage these tools to build complete, end-to-end functioning applications.

How can AI speed up physician responses to patient messages and laboratory results without sacrificing quality?

Dr Albert: AI can distill necessary information efficiently and at scale. However, this does not eliminate the clinician’s responsibility to review AI-interpreted results, summaries, or draft responses. Physicians and other clinicians remain responsible for reviewing, refining, and approving all outputs. Before any communication is finalized, clinicians must serve as the final gatekeeper, governance layer, and validator. This process embodies the human-in-the-loop approach.

What simple safety steps must physicians take to protect patient privacy when using AI tools?

Dr Albert: Commercial platforms must not be used with any protected health information (PHI), as doing so constitutes a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) violation. If a platform processes PHI, an appropriate business associate agreement (BAA) must be in place alongside audit logs and recording measures. When in doubt, data should be de-identified or reviewed with a health information expert to confirm safety before processing. Physicians should always take the necessary steps to safeguard patient data.

How can automated AI pre-visit summaries save physicians time so they can dedicate more attention to their patients?

Dr Albert: Efficiency in the clinic comes down to minutes. Every additional minute spent in the clinic creates administrative debt that accumulates throughout the day. Using AI to summarize chart information, streamline pre-charting, and enhance post-charting communication saves valuable time. Saving seconds or minutes per encounter significantly adds up over the course of a day when seeing 15, 20, 25, or 40 patients, giving clinicians back time that would otherwise be lost.

Dr Albert’s insights connect with those in our report (available here) from Lisa Masson, MD, MBA, FAAFP, FAMIA, Health Sciences Clinical Professor and Medical Director of Enterprise Information Services at Cedars-Sinai, who will be presenting later this week at a Family Physicians meeting. Dr Masson emphasized that while ambient AI scribes and automated documentation tools significantly reduce electronic health record (EHR) burdens, clinicians must remain vigilant gatekeepers against AI errors or hallucinations.

This article originally appeared on The Obesity Advisor
